title: PostgreSQL: scaling writes
description: What to reach for when one node is not enough: vertical scaling, batching, write offloading, partitioning, sharding and connection pooling.
source: Study notes: when and how to use PostgreSQL in system design interviews

questions.prompt: A single node nears its write limit. What is the simplest first lever?

options.text: Bigger hardware: faster NVMe disks for the WAL, more RAM, more cores.
options.why: Right: easy, though rarely the most impressive answer.

options.text: Dropping all constraints from every table.
options.why: That sacrifices integrity for a small gain.

options.text: Moving every table to a different database engine.
options.why: That is a rewrite, not a first step.

options.text: Adding more read replicas to absorb the writes.
options.why: Replicas cannot accept writes in a standard setup.

questions.explanation: Vertical scaling is a fine start, but you should follow it with architectural options.

questions.prompt: Instead of 1,000 single-row inserts you send one multi-row INSERT in one transaction. What is the main risk?

options.text: Writes buffered in the server before the commit are lost if it crashes.
options.why: Right: the batch is the unit of loss.

options.text: The database will refuse any transaction with over ten rows.
options.why: Large batches are normal and supported.

options.text: Indexes stop being maintained during the batch.
options.why: They are maintained, just more efficiently.

options.text: Foreign keys are ignored inside batches.
options.why: Constraints still apply.

questions.explanation: Batching cuts per-transaction overhead. Balance batch size against the data you can afford to lose or replay.

questions.prompt: Which writes are the best candidates for asynchronous offloading through a queue such as Kafka?

options.text: Analytics events and last-seen timestamps, which need no immediate visibility.
options.why: Right: non-critical, latency-tolerant writes.

options.text: The initial payment record for a checkout.
options.why: Money movement needs a synchronous, durable write.

options.text: Account creation that must reject duplicate usernames in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Uniqueness needs an immediate decision from the database.

options.text: Any write that happens inside a multi-table transaction as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Transactions need to stay together in one place.

questions.explanation: Queue the noncritical writes and apply them in batches. Keep correctness-critical writes synchronous.

questions.prompt: Why does time-based partitioning of a posts table help both reads and writes?

options.text: Recent-data queries touch only recent partitions, and index updates stay small.
options.why: Right: smaller scans and per-partition indexes.

options.text: It removes the need for any indexes at all in a typical production setup.
options.why: Partitions still use indexes.

options.text: It spreads the table across several machines automatically without any extra configuration.
options.why: Partitions live in one database; spreading across machines is sharding.

options.text: It makes old data impossible to query.
options.why: Old partitions remain queryable.

questions.explanation: Partitioning suits data with a natural lifecycle. Old partitions can move to cheaper storage or be dropped quickly.

questions.prompt: Users mostly read their own posts. What is a sound shard key for the posts table?

options.text: user_id, so each user's posts live on one shard.
options.why: Right: avoids scatter-gather for the common query.

options.text: A random value per post, to spread load evenly for most everyday workloads.
options.why: It balances writes but forces cross-shard reads of a user's posts.

options.text: The post's created_at date, bucketed by day.
options.why: It sends all new writes to the same hot shard.

options.text: The length of the post content.
options.why: It has no relationship to the access pattern.

questions.explanation: Shard on the column you query by most, and be explicit about the cost of cross-shard queries.

questions.prompt: True or false: PostgreSQL ships with built-in automatic sharding like DynamoDB.

options.text: True
options.why: It does not have automatic built-in sharding.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: manual sharding or Citus.

questions.explanation: You implement sharding yourself, or use a service like Citus that handles much of it.

questions.prompt: Hundreds of application instances open connections and the database slows down. What fits?

options.text: A pooler such as PgBouncer multiplexing many clients onto few connections.
options.why: Right: each connection is a process, so fewer is better.

options.text: Give every application instance a dedicated database process under normal operating conditions.
options.why: That is what overloads memory and CPU.

options.text: Increase max_connections to the number of clients as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: More processes worsen context switching.

options.text: Disable the buffer cache to free memory.
options.why: The cache is central to performance.

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL forks a process per connection, so pooling is essentially mandatory at scale.

questions.prompt: Writes reach 20k per second and the team wants the least complex fix that works. Which ordering of options is most sensible?

options.text: Batching and offloading, then partitioning, then sharding if still needed.
options.why: Right: escalate complexity only when needed.

options.text: Sharding first, since it always solves write scaling in the majority of deployments.
options.why: It adds the most complexity; try cheaper options first.

options.text: Switch databases immediately without measuring without any extra configuration.
options.why: Scale alone is not a justification.

options.text: Add indexes on every column to speed writes.
options.why: More indexes slow writes.

questions.explanation: Start simple, measure, and say what trigger would make you shard.
